newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook--December date and SIB review loom.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook--December date and SIB review loom.

text.p: Metal market trading in the last full week before the Christmas holiday will be dominated by "third Wednesday" pricing and, possibly, the publication of the long-awaited SIB review of the LME, traders said.
Technical tightness for December comes to a head on Monday, with today's cash trading representing business against the key "third Wednesday" - the focal point of current backwardations.
The Securities and Investments Board (SIB) may release the review that the London Metal Exchange (LME) commissioned after the Sumitomo Corp scandal.
"The tendency normally is for things to wind down ahead of Christmas, but this week I think we'll be kept on our toes," one trader said.
Towards the end of last week LME cash/one day backwardations were trading at levels near $23 - which is the market's permissible limit on the daily premium.
The tightness that developed for late-December dates reflected a combination of factors that combined with critically low inventories to exacerbate the LME backwardation.
Traders said short positions rolled forward from June and September sell-offs, end-year book-squaring operations and option requirements all fell on the December date.
Stocks, which were over 275,000 tonnes in September, shrank to 6-1/4 year lows of just 90,500 tonnes last month, although they have since increased to 112,500 tonnes.
"This is still a very, very tight market. I would not be at all surprised if there are some defaults with people unable to deliver warrants," a senior trader said.
Once the December date passes, the overall cash/threes backwardation was expected to continue to ease. On Friday, it was at $100/105, having been as high as $285 in early December.
The three months price ended at $2,132 a tonne on Friday, and is likely to continue ranging in the short term between just below $2,100 and above $2,150, analysts said.
The outcome of the SIB review of the LME will have implications for the whole market and usher in further changes to its trading patterns and strucure.
"It (the LME) had been changing for some years, anyway. Sumitomo and the SIB will probably accelerate that process," one senior trader said.
Industry sources say the SIB may suggest changes, such as daily reporting of inventory movements, revealing ownership of those inventories in warehouses and more transparency on market positions.
Some said that any changes that resulted from the review should go some considerable way to restoring the confidence in the LME that was rocked by the Sumitomo crisis back in June.
